rv.q: This production’s power also depends on the musical performance, which threaded beauty and emotional intensity through so much equivocation.

Against that, there are head-scratching images (who are those giggly young girls in party frocks?) and a hair-shirt refusal to let in the slightest glimpse of colour or beauty. When the magic of Good Friday heralds the spring, do not expect a single daffodil.
The overall result is a mixed show whose strengths outweigh some perverse idiosyncrasies.
Jakub Hrůša tells you immediately why the Royal Opera's orchestral musicians urged him to be appointed Music Director.
Titov's answer is to corrupt the world further and hope the shock passes for insight.
Titov's dreamlike Parsifal manages to infuriate, entertain and provide insight in equal measure.

cn.t: Titov's dystopian Parsifal staging divides critics with its iconoclastic approach, but Hrůša's conducting and strong performances, particularly de Barbeyrac and Gerhaher, earn wide praise in this brutal yet compelling production.
